newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexicans balk at high charges on new pension funds.
newsitem.headline: Mexicans balk at high charges on new pension funds.

text.p: Mexico's new private pension funds have not yet begun to operate, but are already coming under fire for charging high fees to workers and allegedly resorting to dirty tricks in the battle to capture their retirement savings.

The new funds, known as Afores, are slated to begin in July and are expected to rack up $6 billion in savings by year's end, according to Manuel Reynaud, the head of the newly-created Mexican Pension Fund Association and director of Afore Santander-Mexicano, backed by Santander Investment.

Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo and many economists have hailed pension reform as the best way to increase the country's paltry savings rate, create a long-term pool of domestic capital, and develop the country's financial markets.

Critics of the new funds, however, say many workers will actually lose money during the plan's first years until they can build enough savings to offset high commission charges -- which can be up to two percent of a worker's gross salary.
"Afores: Are they worth it?" wondered a recent headline in Mexico City's influential Reforma newspaper.

If a worker invested 10 percent of his salary the first year, about 20 percent of that would go to commission -- giving the worker a loss of about 17 percent in real terms at year's end, the newspaper estimated.

Opposition National Action Party (PAN) Senator Jose Angel Conchello recently criticized the high fees and estimated the Afores will make some 8 billion pesos, about $1 billion, in commissions alone during the first year.

And some pension fund companies have been accused by Mexico's largest labor group, the Mexican Labor Confederation (CTM), of handing out money and other gifts to workers in exchange for a pledge to sign up their savings, a violation of the law regulating the new system.
Pension fund managers on Monday denied any wrongdoing, but said the association would soon be coming out with a "code of ethics" to guide competition.

They also said the commissions, necessary to offset the high cost of recruiting workers, were lower than in countries such as Chile and Argentina and lower than the real costs of Mexico's virtually bankrupt pay-as-you-go public system.
According to the fund managers, the majority of workers with some sort of existing savings will get real returns their first year.

"This is a totally transparent system...The previous system had many hidden costs," Reynaud told reporters. "It's not fair to judge this system on the first year. (The commissions) will not be an issue in two years' time."
One pension fund, run by Inbursa financial group, has taken a contrarian view, however -- charging its customers a commission on real returns only.
"We simply did not think it made sense to ask a worker to put in 100 pesos and take 25 pesos away immediately," said Roberto Isaac Rodriguez, the director of Afore Inbursa.
Isaac Rodriguez said Inbursa is the first private pension fund manager in Latin America to scrap the automatic commission system in favor of a profit-based charge.

Reynaud said the commission as a percentage of a workers' salary will fall to roughly 1.67 percent after 25 years and 1.12 percent after 35 years. He added that the level of commission will also be market driven in the future as competitive pressures increase.
"This is the first and only time the companies will set the level of commissions," he said.
